text: Some time later David defeated the Philistines and subdued them, taking Gath and its surrounding villages out of Philistine hands.
He also defeated Moab, and the Moabites became David's subjects and paid him tribute.
David defeated Hadadezer king of Zobah, as far as Hamath, when Hadadezer marched out to establish his power along the Euphrates River.

versions.text: David defeated Hadadezer king of Zobah, near Hamath, when Hadadezer marched out to establish his power as far as the Euphrates River.
versions.explanation: The directional form חֲמָתָה indicates movement or extent ("toward/as far as Hamath") rather than mere proximity; "near Hamath" understates the geographic reach of the campaign. Also, בִּנְהַר־פְּרָת is literally "at/along the Euphrates River," which the revised wording preserves while keeping the natural spoken rhythm.

text: David captured from him a thousand chariots, seven thousand horsemen, and twenty thousand foot soldiers. He hamstrung all the chariot horses, but kept a hundred chariots for himself.

versions.text: David captured from him a thousand chariots, seven thousand charioteers, and twenty thousand foot soldiers. He hamstrung all the chariot horses except a hundred, which he kept.
versions.explanation: פָּרָשִׁים normally denotes mounted horsemen, a category distinct from the chariots already listed; rendering it "charioteers" blurs the three-part listing of chariots, cavalry, and infantry.

versions.text: David captured from him a thousand chariots, seven thousand horsemen, and twenty thousand foot soldiers. He hamstrung all the chariot horses except a hundred, which he kept.
versions.explanation: In the Hebrew the hundred that David spared are explicitly "a hundred chariots" (מֵאָה רָכֶב), not a hundred horses. As written, "except a hundred" most naturally attaches to "chariot horses," obscuring what was retained. Naming the chariots keeps the accounting clear and reads smoothly aloud.

text: When the Arameans of Damascus came to help Hadadezer king of Zobah, David struck down twenty-two thousand of them.
He stationed garrisons in Aram of Damascus, and the Arameans became his subjects and paid him tribute. So the LORD gave David victory wherever he went.
David took the gold shields carried by Hadadezer's officers and brought them to Jerusalem.
From Tibhath and Cun, cities of Hadadezer, David took a great quantity of bronze, which Solomon later used to make the bronze Sea, the pillars, and the bronze vessels.
When Tou king of Hamath heard that David had defeated the entire army of Hadadezer king of Zobah,
he sent his son Hadoram to King David to greet him and congratulate him on his victory over Hadadezer, who had been at war with Tou. Hadoram brought all kinds of articles of gold, silver, and bronze.
King David dedicated these to the LORD, along with the silver and gold he had carried off from all the nations—from Edom, Moab, the Ammonites, the Philistines, and the Amalekites.
Abishai son of Zeruiah struck down eighteen thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt.
David stationed garrisons in Edom, and all the Edomites became his subjects. So the LORD gave David victory wherever he went.

versions.text: He stationed garrisons in Edom, and all the Edomites became David's subjects. So the LORD gave David victory wherever he went.
versions.explanation: Because the preceding verse names Abishai as the actor, the pronoun "He" is ambiguous when read aloud; naming David clarifies the subject, as the rest of the verse makes clear.

text: David reigned over all Israel, governing his whole people with justice and righteousness.
Joab son of Zeruiah commanded the army; Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was recorder;
Zadok son of Ahitub and Abimelech son of Abiathar were priests; Shavsha was secretary;
Benaiah son of Jehoiada was over the Kerethites and Pelethites; and David's sons were the chief officials at the king's side.
